transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Enhancers & 3D genome, for Monday, November 23.
Let's turn to Enhancers and 3D genome. The headline is a medRxiv preprint from the Amundadottir lab, asking which genes sit behind the non-coding risk loci for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Earlier GWAS found 31 risk signals across 26 loci, but the causal variants and target genes are still mostly unknown. The authors fine-mapped 1,414 variants. Then they used a capture-based conformation method called GWAS Capture-C to see which promoters those variants physically contact.

That nominated 273 candidate genes at 25 loci, some over long distances. They include contacts of more than a megabase with KRT gene promoters and about 280 kilobases with SOX9, a master regulator of pancreatic development.
The strongest case is at 7p14.1. There's an eQTL for INHBA, a roughly 900 kilobase contact with its promoter, and CRISPR inhibition at four fine-mapped variants lowered INHBA expression.

So the contact, the eQTL and the perturbation all point to a distal enhancer. The caution is that 273 genes is a list of candidates, only one locus got functional follow-up, and this is still a preprint.

Next, a bioRxiv preprint from the Villasenor lab introduces Read&Tag. It's a CUT&Tag-style method that fuses engineered chromatin reader domains or intrabodies directly to Tn5, so no antibodies are needed.

It profiles histone marks, DNA methylation and elongating RNA polymerase two, even in frozen tissue and low-input samples. The neat part is a dual-specificity reader that only tagments fragments carrying both H3K4 trimethylation and H3K27 trimethylation. That means bivalency is measured directly instead of inferred from overlapping profiles.
Barcoded complexes also read four chromatin features in one reaction, though it still needs independent benchmarking.
In Plant Cell, the Li lab traces the very high ripening expression of the pepper CCS gene to a super-enhancer-like array of 22 CArG-box repeats, where activation scales with repeat copy number.
And in GigaByte, the Ji lab shares single-nucleus ATAC-seq of healing rat skin wounds over 19 days, with 37,555 nuclei across 23 cell types.
The takeaway is that linking non-coding variants to target genes now takes contact maps plus perturbation, not contacts alone.
